standard.title: Characters, sentence structures and syntax
standard.description: use components and/or characters, sentence structures, syntax and writing system features to infer meaning and to compose and respond to familiar and some unfamiliar texts and contexts
standard.prior_knowledge: Students entering at Y7-8 have variable literacy in the target language writing system — ranging from strong character recognition from home literacy to limited exposure. They have oral syntactic knowledge but have not necessarily analysed sentence structures explicitly, applied stroke order systematically, or used morphological knowledge to infer meaning in unfamiliar texts.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students use component and character knowledge, sentence structures and writing system features to infer meaning and compose a range of familiar and some unfamiliar texts.

nodes.label: Character analysis and morphological inference
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can analyse character components and morphemes to infer meaning, identify radicals and their placement, and recognise relationships between characters sharing common components.
nodes.minimum_width: Identify the components of at least five characters, explain how the component contributes to meaning or sound, and infer the meaning of at least two unfamiliar characters using component knowledge.
nodes.typical_width: Identify the nature, arrangement and function of components in characters; infer meanings from component analysis; identify placement patterns for specific radicals; analyse how morphemes relate across words; recognise auspicious character combinations; compare simplified and traditional character forms.
wider: Investigate a semantic component family — all characters sharing a specific radical — and explain the semantic or phonetic pattern connecting them
Predict the meaning of a set of unfamiliar characters using component analysis, verify using a dictionary, and evaluate the accuracy of morphological inference across the set
nodes.hinge_reason: Morphological inference is the prerequisite for independent reading of unfamiliar texts. Entry students with home literacy may recognise many characters but have not analysed the component system — without this analysis they cannot extend vocabulary strategically.

response_modes.reason: Component analysis requires systematic application of a framework. Explicit instruction on component types, radical placement patterns, and morphological relationships builds the analytical capacity before students can infer independently.

success_criteria: Identifies components of at least five characters with explanation of their contribution
Infers the meaning of at least two unfamiliar characters using component knowledge

nodes.label: Writing system conventions and sentence construction
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can apply stroke order and direction rules, use punctuation correctly, and construct a range of sentence types — affirmative, negative, interrogative, imperative — using cohesive devices.
nodes.minimum_width: Write at least five characters with correct stroke order, and produce at least three sentences using different sentence types with correct punctuation.
nodes.typical_width: Apply stroke order and direction when writing characters; use digital tools for unknown characters; use punctuation conventions; construct affirmative, negative, interrogative and imperative sentences; join, contrast and sequence using cohesive devices; use complement, extent and direction constructions.
wider: Investigate running script or cursive forms of familiar characters — compare with standard printed forms and discuss the relationship between form and function
Create an annotated sentence analysis — label every grammatical component using metalanguage and explain the contribution of each to the overall meaning

response_modes.reason: Writing system conventions and sentence construction require repeated production practice. Regular writing tasks with attention to stroke order, punctuation and varied sentence types build the accurate productive competence needed.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: Entry students with strong oral grammar often produce sentence structures correctly in speech but have not applied them in formal writing. Width investment here bridges oral and written grammatical competence — making implicit knowledge explicit and accurate in written production.
success_criteria: Writes at least five characters with correct stroke order
Produces at least three sentences using different sentence types with correct punctuation

nodes.label: Composing and responding to unfamiliar texts
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can apply full character and syntactic knowledge to compose and respond to texts in some unfamiliar contexts, using morphological inference and writing system knowledge strategically.
nodes.minimum_width: Compose a text of at least eight sentences on a familiar or moderately unfamiliar topic applying full writing system knowledge and at least three grammatical structures.
nodes.typical_width: Apply character and grammatical knowledge to compose and respond to texts across familiar and some unfamiliar contexts; use morphological knowledge to approach unfamiliar vocabulary; apply cohesive devices and complex sentence constructions; differentiate morphemes with similar forms to enhance communication.
wider: Compose a text on an unfamiliar topic using morphological inference and contextual strategies — document the strategies used and evaluate their effectiveness
Analyse own extended writing for grammatical accuracy — identify patterns of error and develop a targeted revision plan

response_modes.reason: Composing and responding to unfamiliar texts integrates morphological inference (node 1) and writing system conventions (node 2) into full productive literacy engagement. The teaching investment is in creating text composition tasks with genuine unfamiliar elements that require strategic deployment of both skills.

success_criteria: Composes a text of at least eight sentences applying writing system knowledge throughout
Uses at least three grammatical structures correctly across the text
